extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history, media studies researchers, and readers interested in the development of American newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts standards and evaluative dimensions used to characterize and judge newspapers in New York in the 1890s, especially the contrasting 'story' (entertainment/sensational) and 'information' (decontextualized/verifiable) models. Includes business, stylistic, moral, and audience-oriented criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story ideal (aesthetic/entertainment function)
rubrics_metrics.description: When telling stories is taken to be the role of the newspaper — an 'aesthetic' function: the news serves primarily to create satisfying aesthetic experiences which help readers interpret their lives; 'the reporter is generally sent out to get a story, not the facts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes selection and framing of facts to produce enjoyable or meaningful narratives for readers; associated with the World and Journal, appeals to working-class and newly urban/immigrant audiences; manifested in features, romantic fiction, vivid human-interest pieces, and layout choices that highlight drama rather than decontextualized facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information ideal (decontextualized, prompt verifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information as a distinct form of communication that 'lays claim to prompt verifiability' and aims to be 'understandable in itself' — an ideal of providing unframed facts or 'information' rather than stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with the New York Times and the educated middle class; stresses verifiability and decontextualization (what Gouldner calls 'decontextualized' communication and Bernstein's 'elaborated code'); seen as incompatible with storytelling but prized for apparent reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness, objectivity, scrupulous dispassion
rubrics_metrics.description: The informational ideal is associated with fairness, objectivity, and scrupulous dispassion — newspapers stressing information tend to be seen as more reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text questions who judges reliability and cautions that adherence to an informational model does not guarantee factual accuracy; the association with objectivity develops over time into an explicit journalistic ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and self-advertisement (style over substance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensationalism defined less by subject matter than by style: extravagant display of news (large headlines, illustrations, cartoons), self-promotion, and turning news itself into advertising for the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: World and Journal's use of illustrations, two-column screaming headlines, boasting of circulation figures; self-advertising includes layout choices and exclusive feature promotion; considered effective for growing circulation but criticized as undermining professional dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation and advertising as measures of newspaper worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation became the public/audited indicator of a newspaper's competitive standing and the commodity sold to advertisers; advertising revenue grew to dominate newspaper income.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices such as selling ad space on the basis of circulation, standardizing rates, and working with agencies (Rowell directory, open contracts, ANPA) shaped editorial decisions; newspapers were judged by advertisers as well as readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper functions: inform, interpret, entertain
rubrics_metrics.description: A tripartite functional standard: newspapers should inform, interpret, and entertain (Melville Stone's formulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different papers weighted these functions differently (Times emphasizing information/interpretation; World emphasizing entertainment); evaluating a paper involves assessing its balance among these functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the news 'all the news...concise and attractive...impartially'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adolph Ochs' explicit statement of journalistic standards: 'give the news, all the news, in concise and attractive form, in language that is parliamentary in good society...to give the news impartially, without fear or favor...to make the columns...a forum...and...invite intelligent discussion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes informational ideals: timeliness ('as early...as any other reliable medium'), impartiality, civility of language, comprehensiveness, and fostering public debate. Serves as an explicit production/evaluation checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism vs. commercialism (self-advertising undermines professional standing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more a newspaper self-advertises, the less it appears to maintain a 'professional' standing; heavy self-promotion is likened to behaviors distrusted in professional relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to prohibitions on advertising among lawyers/physicians: excessive boasting or layout designed to sell the paper can be judged as unprofessional and morally suspect by contemporaries and elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to audience literacy, language, and class (readability & features)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial and stylistic choices should be adapted to readers' language skills, literacy, and social location — e.g., simple words and sentence structures, illustrations and cartoons, women's pages, and features that match readers' interests and capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulitzer's World simplified language and used illustrations to attract immigrants and less literate readers; Sunday editions and features (fashion, etiquette, advice columns) targeted women and consumers; price (penny paper) and format choices are part of audience adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of crusades and civic campaigns as editorial strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained crusades and political exposés used both as genuine civic engagement and as tools to stimulate circulation and self-promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulitzer's development of the newspaper crusade (headlines, exposés) served editorial aims and circulation growth (e.g., fundraising for the Statue of Liberty pedestal); evaluating papers considers whether such campaigns serve public interest or primarily boost the paper's brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence and verification of reporting (memory and follow-up)
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional reporting includes independent follow-up and verification rather than merely repeating competitors' accounts (Times example: interviewing Cuban women at the dock and publishing its own account without referencing earlier sensational reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence of sourcing and verification practices are signals of a paper's adherence to informational/professional norms; omission of sourcing or reliance on hearsay counts against rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and class judgment as part of newspaper evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers and critics judge newspapers not only on empirical criteria but morally — associating the informational model with middle-class respectability and the story model with working-class entertainment; 'respectability' becomes a criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of 'decency', 'dignity', and social approval shaped perceptions of quality; this shows that evaluations of journalism are entangled with social-class values rather than purely objective standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emerging ideal of objectivity as an ideological reflex
rubrics_metrics.description: While 'objectivity' was not yet the explicit term in the 1890s, a later century-wide move made objectivity an ideological standard — skepticism about neutral facts led to objectivity as an ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text situates objectivity's later rise in broader cultural shifts (democratic market society, utilitarian culture, skepticism from thinkers like Nietzsche and Freud). For evaluation, this warns that 'information' alone did not equal objectivity and that objectivity became codified later.
